title: Secatogue Ancestral Land
summary: Secatogue ancestry belongs to the creeks, meadows and shores of Great South Bay, where Native life long preceded colonial towns. Land transactions and settlement restricted that homeland and changed how its people appeared in written records. A less visible name is not evidence that a people vanished. This bay remains part of a living Native landscape, including neighboring Unkechaug and Shinnecock communities whose histories extend beyond reservation boundaries.
why_this_matters: Secatogue Ancestral Land presents Great South Bay creeks, marshes, and inland routes as Native geography. It also connects older records to descendant community memory and the continued presence of Native families on Long Island.
introduction_title: Secatogue homeland along Great South Bay
introduction_content:
The National Park Service identifies Secatogue people among the ancestral communities of the Great South Bay and Fire Island region. The historical records below connect the name to shore, creek and meadow places and to relationships with neighboring Native leaders. Colonial land records are evidence of pressure on a homeland, not a complete record of the people who belonged to it.

The present Unkechaug community at Poospatuck and the Shinnecock Nation make Native continuance visible in this wider coastal region. Their presence does not establish that every Secatogue family became part of either nation. It does make the familiar story of an entirely vanished Native South Shore untenable. Honoring Secatogue ancestry includes protecting the bay and cultural places and making room for family histories that an archive organized around colonial deeds may not preserve.

Sources for ancestry and continuance: National Park Service; Shinnecock Indian Nation. See References for citations and the historical sources used below.

Secatogue People And Great South Bay

Secatogue is one of the names repeated in the old "thirteen tribes" list, but historian John A. Strong's critique of that framework cautions against reading the list as a complete pre-contact political map. The name is best understood as a place-based record of people living in relation to bay, creek, meadow, and inland routes, not as a complete description of government. The people behind the name were not confined to the neat borders that deeds and later maps tried to impose. Their histories continued through kinship, movement, land records, descendant memory, and relationships with neighboring communities.
history_content: The name Sichetanyhacky appears in Dutch-period records as a land or country name for the Secatogue people. It is tied to the eastern boundary of Massapeag jurisdiction and to Secatogue territory on the south shore.
translation_content: Sichetanyhacky is interpreted as the country or land of the Secatogues. Recorded forms include Siketenwhacky, Siketenhacky, and Sickentanhacky.
preservation_content: Some Secatogue histories involve camps, village sites, family places, and archaeological traces. The public story stays at the level of the broader south shore landscape.
land_loss_content: Secatogue history is tied to south shore tidal creeks, bay travel, colonial deed records, community gatherings, and later descendant history. Land records and colonial restrictions show Native presence under increasing pressure rather than disappearance.
geometry_cleanup_notes: The Babylon/Islip south-shore mainland, Great South Bay-facing necks and marsh islands, Captree/Robert Moses land, and western Fire Island. This corrects the former mainland-only display but does not claim a precise territorial line through Great South Bay or Fire Island.
